screens.title: Managing System Services (systemd)
screens.narratorSegment: In modern Linux systems, systemd is the init system and service manager that brings your system to life and keeps services running. In this lesson you'll learn what a unit is, why service unit files matter, and how the systemctl and journalctl tools let you control and inspect services. We'll ground this in practical actions: starting and stopping daemons, enabling services at boot, reading service logs, and creating a minimal custom service that runs a simple script. You'll also learn the key safety practices, like why you must avoid stopping critical services remotely without a backup access method. These skills matter because services provide the running pieces of your system — web servers, SSH, databases — and managing them reliably is a daily admin task. By the end you'll be able to inspect a service's status, interpret its logs to diagnose failures, and write a basic service unit, then reload systemd so your changes take effect.

These are not theoretical items; you will practice them in guided steps, and you will also learn common pitfalls like forgetting to run daemon-reload or stopping SSH remotely without a fallback. These competencies prepare you to manage daemons reliably in production and test environments.

screens.title: What is systemd and what are units?
screens.narratorSegment: Systemd is the init system and service manager used by most modern Linux distributions. At boot it runs as PID 1 and orchestrates the system's services, sockets, mount points, and targets. The central abstraction in systemd is a unit: a configuration file that represents a managed resource. Units come in many types — service, target, mount, device, socket — but as an administrator you will mostly work with service units. A. service unit declares how a daemon starts, stops, and integrates with boot targets. For example, a web server package installs an nginx. service file that contains an ExecStart line and any dependencies. A common misconception is that systemd itself is just a process monitor. It is more: it manages dependencies, ordering, and parallel startup and offers a unified interface for control and inspection. Understanding units helps you reason about startup order, failures, and overrides. Consider the example of network. target: if a service needs networking, including After=network. target in its unit ensures systemd waits for that target before starting the service. Reflect: which services on your system require network. target to be present before they run?

keyIdea.text: A unit is the systemd configuration file that models resources; .service files describe how daemons run and depend on other targets.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › What is systemd?
Systemd: the init system
It boots the system, manages dependencies, and exposes a unified control interface via systemctl.
Unit: the central concept
A unit file models a resource. Service units end in .service and define ExecStart, dependencies, and install targets.
Why it matters
Units let you control lifecycle, order startup, and attach logging. They are the contract between systemd and the daemon.
Common misconception
Systemd is not just a monitor. It manages dependencies, parallelization, and targets that group units.
Concrete example
An nginx.service provided by a package includes ExecStart to launch the server and After=network.target so networking is up first.
Key Takeaway

A unit file is the canonical way to tell systemd how to manage a resource; .service units manage daemons.

Check your understanding
Name one dependency a service might declare and why it matters.

screens.title: Unit file locations and precedence
screens.narratorSegment: Service unit files can originate from packages or from local administrator edits, and their location determines which file systemd uses. Packaged unit files are typically installed under /usr/lib/systemd/system. Local or custom unit files, along with deliberate overrides, reside in /etc/systemd/system. When both locations contain a unit with the same name, files under /etc take precedence. This lets you customize behavior without editing package files, preserving upgrade safety. A common mistake is editing /usr/lib/service files directly; updates can overwrite your changes. Another useful location is /run/systemd/system for runtime units generated on the fly. Practically, when you create or edit a unit under /etc, always run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd rereads the files. If you forget daemon-reload you may see the old behavior and wonder why your changes didn't apply. Example: if nginx. service exists in both /usr/lib and /etc, the version in /etc will be used by systemd and symlinks in multi-user. target. wants will point to the effective unit. Unit file locations and precedence means /etc/systemd/system overrides /usr/lib/systemd/system; use /etc for customizations and run daemon-reload after edits.. In practical terms, where unit files live and which ones win when duplicated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Unit locations
Location comparison
/usr/lib/systemd/system
Packaged unit files from distribution packages.
/etc/systemd/system
Administrator overrides and custom units. This location wins when names collide.
/run/systemd/system
Runtime, transient units created while system is running.
Example scenario
You place a modified my.service in /etc/systemd/system. systemd will use that file instead of the one in /usr/lib. Run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so the new file is recognized.
Common mistake

Editing /usr/lib files risks being overwritten by updates. Use /etc for customizations and prefer drop-in overrides when possible.

Key Takeaway

/etc overrides /usr/lib. Always run daemon-reload after changes; otherwise systemd won't see new or modified units.

screens.title: Common systemctl commands
screens.narratorSegment: The systemctl tool is the primary interface for interacting with systemd. Learn a small set of commands that cover most tasks. Use systemctl start service to start a service immediately. Use systemctl stop service to stop it. Restart restarts a service, useful after a configuration change that cannot be reloaded. Reload asks the service to re-read its configuration without fully restarting; not every service supports reload. Use systemctl enable service to configure the service to start at boot; this creates a symlink under multi-user. target. wants. systemctl disable prevents automatic start at boot. To check runtime state, use systemctl status service which shows active/inactive, PID, recent journal lines, and whether the unit is enabled. Two helpful queries are systemctl is-active and systemctl is-enabled; they return concise information suited for scripts. A common confusion is thinking enable also starts the service immediately — enable only affects boot. If you want it running now, run start as well. Practice combining these commands when managing a sample service to internalize the lifecycle. Common systemctl commands means systemctl start/stop/restart/reload control runtime state; enable/disable control boot behavior; status and is-active/is-enabled report state.. In practical terms, start, stop, restart, reload, and check state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › systemctl commands
Common commands
Start
systemctl start <service> — run now.
Stop
systemctl stop <service> — stop now.
Restart
systemctl restart <service> — stop then start.
Reload
systemctl reload <service> — re-read config if supported.
Enable vs Start
Enable configures boot behavior by creating symlinks; it does not start the service immediately. To run now, use start in addition to enable.
Quick checks
  • systemctl status <service> — shows activity, PID, and recent logs.
  • systemctl is-active <service> — script-friendly active check.
  • systemctl is-enabled <service> — shows boot enablement.
Key Takeaway

Use start/stop/restart for runtime control, enable/disable for boot behavior, and status/is-active to verify results.

screens.title: Inspecting status with systemctl status
screens.narratorSegment: systemctl status is the first command to run when a service misbehaves. It gives a concise snapshot: whether the unit is active or inactive, the main process PID, memory usage, and a few recent journal entries. Use this output to determine immediate causes, such as a crash on startup or a failed dependency. An important skill is reading the status summary and then following up with journalctl -u service for detailed logs. A common misinterpretation is assuming an inactive state always means the service crashed; some services stop after completing a oneshot task. Look at Type= in the unit to understand expected behavior. For example, if a service uses Type=forking, the main process may detach and status will show the child PID. Always combine status with the unit file and logs to build a diagnosis. Try running status, note the PID and recent messages, then open the journal to see complete entries for that unit. Inspecting status with systemctl status means systemctl status gives a quick diagnostic snapshot; use it with journalctl for full logs and unit file inspection for context.. In practical terms, interpret pid, active state, and journal excerpts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › systemctl status
Sample output (annotated)
● sshd.service - OpenSSH server daemon
   Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service; enabled; vendor preset: enabled)
   Active: active (running) since Tue 2024-01-01 10:00:00; 1h 23min ago
 Main PID: 1234 (sshd)
    Tasks: 1 (limit: 4915)
   Memory: 4.3M
    CGroup: /system.slice/sshd.service
            └─1234 /usr/sbin/sshd -D

Jan 01 10:00:00 host systemd[1]: Started OpenSSH server daemon.
Jan 01 10:01:05 host sshd[1234]: Accepted password for user from 10.0.0.1 port 54321 ssh2
What to look for
  • Loaded: where the unit file came from and whether it's enabled.
  • Active: the current runtime state and how long it has been running.
  • Main PID and CGroup: the running process identifier and control group path.
  • Recent journal lines included at the bottom for quick context.
Misconception
An inactive state may be expected for oneshot units; check the unit's Type setting before assuming a crash.
Key Takeaway

Start troubleshooting with status, then run journalctl -u <service> for a complete log history.

screens.title: Viewing service logs with journalctl
screens.narratorSegment: When systemctl status provides a brief window into recent events, journalctl supplies the full log history for a unit. Use journalctl -u service to see all messages generated by that service. You can add -n 20 to show the last twenty lines or --since to restrict by time. These logs include stdout and stderr emitted by the daemon plus messages from systemd itself. This makes journalctl indispensable for diagnosing why a service failed during startup or why it repeatedly restarted. For example, if your custom service exits immediately, journalctl -u my-custom-service will show the script errors or exit codes. A common mistake is reading general system logs instead of the unit-specific ones; always pass -u with the unit name when troubleshooting a service. Combine journalctl with systemctl status to form a fast triage loop: read status for immediate context, then use journalctl for deeper detail. Example commands
# Show entire log for a unit
journalctl -u my-custom-service

# Show the last 20 lines
journalctl -u my-custom-service -n 20

# Show logs since one hour ago
journalctl -u my-custom-service --since "1 hour ago"

If my-custom-service fails immediately, journalctl -u my-custom-service will show the script error line or missing executable path, guiding your fix.

screens.title: Service unit file structure
screens.narratorSegment: A typical. service file contains three main sections that tell systemd how to treat the service. The [Unit] section holds metadata such as Description= and dependency directives like After= and Requires=. Use After= to ensure the service starts after a given target, for example After=network. target. The [Service] section defines the runtime behavior. Key directives include Type= to describe the process model, ExecStart= for the start command, ExecStop= or ExecReload= when needed, WorkingDirectory= to set the process working directory, and User= or Group= to drop privileges. The Restart= directive controls automatic restarts, for example Restart=on-failure. The [Install] section specifies how the unit is enabled; WantedBy=multi-user. target will make the service start in the typical multi-user environment. A common oversight is placing ExecStart without a full path; always provide the absolute path to avoid PATH-related failures. Reading and editing these three sections gives you direct control over service lifecycle and security. Service unit file structure means service units use [unit] for metadata, [service] for runtime commands and permissions, and [install] for enablement targets.. In practical terms, understand [unit], [service], and [install] sections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Description=, After=, Requires= and other dependency lines.

screens.title: Key directives: ExecStart, Type, User, Restart
screens.narratorSegment: Within the [Service] section a few directives determine how a service runs and how systemd treats it. ExecStart is the command systemd runs to start the service; it should be a full path to the executable or script. Type tells systemd how the service behaves on startup. Type=simple assumes the process stays in the foreground; Type=forking expects the service to fork and background itself; Type=oneshot is for short-lived tasks. User and Group drop privileges so the service runs as a non-root account when appropriate, increasing security. Restart controls automatic restarts; Restart=on-failure restarts only on error exits, while Restart=always will restart for any exit. Choosing improper combinations causes confusion: for example, using Type=forking but pointing ExecStart to a script that does not fork will lead to incorrect PID detection. Always pair your Type setting with the actual process model of the daemon. Example: a simple logging script used as a service often uses Type=simple and runs in the foreground so systemd can manage it cleanly. Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Service directives
Core [Service] directives
ExecStart=
Absolute command to launch the service.
Type=
Process model: simple, forking, oneshot, etc. Must match how the daemon behaves.
User= / Group=
Run the service as a non-root user when possible for security.
Restart=
Controls automatic restart behavior, e.g., on-failure or always.
Concrete example
A foreground script should use Type=simple. If you set Type=forking for a non-forking script, systemd may report the wrong PID and mismanage the unit.
Security note
Prefer User= to run services with least privilege. Root should be used only when necessary.
Key Takeaway

Match Type to process behavior, use ExecStart with absolute paths, and choose Restart and User wisely for reliability and security.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's create a minimal custom service that appends timestamps to a log file. In [Install], use WantedBy=multi-user. target so enabling pulls it into the multi-user boot target. After saving the unit file, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd sees the new unit. keyIdea.text: Write an executable script, create a .service unit in /etc, run daemon-reload, then start and inspect the service.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Create custom service
Script (make executable)
#!/bin/bash
# /usr/local/bin/my-custom-script.sh

echo "$(date): My custom service is running!" >> /tmp/my-custom-service.log
Then run: sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/my-custom-script.sh
Unit file (/etc/systemd/system/my-custom-service.service)
[Unit]
Description=My Custom Cohortia Service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/my-custom-script.sh
Type=simple
Restart=on-failure
User=root
Group=root

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Apply and test
Run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then sudo systemctl start my-custom-service. Verify with systemctl status and check /tmp/my-custom-service.log.
Key Takeaway

A simple script plus a small unit file demonstrates how systemd manages custom services end-to-end.

screens.title: Daemon-reload and a common troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent source of confusion is making changes to unit files and then not seeing those changes take effect. After creating or editing any unit under /etc or elsewhere, you must run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd rereads its configuration files. Without this reload, systemd continues to use its cached view and will not know about new units or modifications. If a unit still fails to start after daemon-reload, follow this checklist: 1) Run systemctl status to get the short diagnostic. 2) Run journalctl -u to read detailed logs. 3) Inspect the unit file for absolute paths in ExecStart and correct Type. 4) Check file permissions and the executable bit on scripts. 5) If you enabled the service, confirm the symlink under multi-user. target. wants. A common operational mistake is enabling a broken unit and then rebooting, which can lead to boot-time failures. For custom or critical services, test start/stop behavior locally before enabling at boot. Daemon-reload and a common troubleshooting checklist means always run daemon-reload after edits. use status, journalctl, file inspection, and permission checks to diagnose persistent failures.. In practical terms, what to do when changes don't appear to take effect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › daemon-reload & troubleshooting
Reload and checklist
Always run sudo systemctl daemon-reload after creating or changing unit files so systemd sees your edits.
Checklist when a unit won't start:
  1. systemctl status <unit> for quick context
  2. journalctl -u <unit> for full logs
  3. Verify ExecStart has an absolute path and correct permissions
  4. Confirm Type matches the process model
  5. Check enablement symlinks under multi-user.target.wants if necessary
Concrete example
If your service still runs the old command after you edit ExecStart, you most likely forgot to run sudo systemctl daemon-reload. Running reload then restart makes the new command active.
Warning
Enabling a badly configured unit may cause boot issues. Test starting locally before enabling for boot.
Key Takeaway

daemon-reload is essential after edits. Use the checklist to triage failures systematically.

screens.title: Safety practices and cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: Managing services requires awareness of operational risk. The most important safety tip is never to stop or disable critical services like sshd when you have no alternative access to the machine. If you are connected over SSH and you stop sshd, you will be disconnected and may be locked out. Always have a secondary access method, such as a console or out-of-band management, before touching remote-critical services. When you create a temporary service for testing, plan a cleanup path: sudo systemctl stop my-custom-service, sudo systemctl disable my-custom-service, then remove the script and unit file from /usr/local/bin and /etc/systemd/system. Finally run sudo systemctl daemon-reload to purge the removed unit from systemd's view. A common mistake is leaving test services enabled which will persist across reboots. Cleaning up prevents unexpected behavior later and keeps system targets uncluttered. Think through the impact of each enable or disable action before running the command on production systems. Safety practices and cleanup means never stop or disable critical remote services without fallback access. clean up test units and always daemon-reload after removal.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Safety & cleanup
Safety rules
  • Do not stop or disable sshd when connected remotely unless you have alternate access.
  • Test services locally in a VM or console before enabling at boot.
  • Document enable/disable actions so others know why the change was made.
Cleanup steps
Stop the service: sudo systemctl stop my-custom-service
Disable it from boot: sudo systemctl disable my-custom-service
Remove files: sudo rm /usr/local/bin/my-custom-script.sh and sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/my-custom-service.service
Reload systemd: sudo systemctl daemon-reload
Reflection
Before changing a critical service, ask: do I have console access or a fallback? If not, schedule maintenance or use a test environment.

fullNarratorScript:
In modern Linux systems, systemd is the init system and service manager that brings your system to life and keeps services running. In this lesson you'll learn what a unit is, why service unit files matter, and how the systemctl and journalctl tools let you control and inspect services. We'll ground this in practical actions: starting and stopping daemons, enabling services at boot, reading service logs, and creating a minimal custom service that runs a simple script. You'll also learn the key safety practices, like why you must avoid stopping critical services remotely without a backup access method. These skills matter because services provide the running pieces of your system — web servers, SSH, databases — and managing them reliably is a daily admin task. By the end you'll be able to inspect a service's status, interpret its logs to diagnose failures, and write a basic service unit, then reload systemd so your changes take effect.

These objectives map directly to day-to-day tasks you'll perform as a systems administrator. First, you'll understand systemd's role as the init system and how units model system resources. Second, you'll learn to use systemctl to start, stop, restart, and reload services safely. Third, you'll be able to locate and interpret service unit files and know how the precedence between /usr/lib and /etc affects overrides. Fourth, you'll inspect service states and recent events using systemctl status and journalctl to diagnose failures. Each objective pairs a clear practical action with why it matters. For example, enabling a web server ensures it survives reboots, while reading journal logs explains why a service failed to start. These are not theoretical items; you will practice them in guided steps, and you will also learn common pitfalls like forgetting to run daemon-reload or stopping SSH remotely without a fallback. These competencies prepare you to manage daemons reliably in production and test environments.

These additional objectives focus on practical checks and safe administration. You will learn to check whether a service is enabled at boot, and recognize the difference between starting a service for the current session and enabling it for future boots. You will understand the precedence of unit file locations so you can safely override packaged units by placing edited files in /etc/systemd/system. You will also adopt safety practices to avoid losing remote access when managing sshd or other critical services. Finally, you will be able to clean up temporary services and restore the system by disabling and removing custom unit files. Each competence is paired with a small verification action, like running systemctl is-enabled or checking multi-user. target. wants, so you can confirm your change behaved as expected. Learning Objectives (continued) means master the enable/disable lifecycle, unit file precedence, and safety checks to avoid accidental lockout.. In practical terms, additional practical competencies and safety checks. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Systemd is the init system and service manager used by most modern Linux distributions. At boot it runs as PID 1 and orchestrates the system's services, sockets, mount points, and targets. The central abstraction in systemd is a unit: a configuration file that represents a managed resource. Units come in many types — service, target, mount, device, socket — but as an administrator you will mostly work with service units. A. service unit declares how a daemon starts, stops, and integrates with boot targets. For example, a web server package installs an nginx. service file that contains an ExecStart line and any dependencies. A common misconception is that systemd itself is just a process monitor. It is more: it manages dependencies, ordering, and parallel startup and offers a unified interface for control and inspection. Understanding units helps you reason about startup order, failures, and overrides. Consider the example of network. target: if a service needs networking, including After=network. target in its unit ensures systemd waits for that target before starting the service. Reflect: which services on your system require network. target to be present before they run?

Service unit files can originate from packages or from local administrator edits, and their location determines which file systemd uses. Packaged unit files are typically installed under /usr/lib/systemd/system. Local or custom unit files, along with deliberate overrides, reside in /etc/systemd/system. When both locations contain a unit with the same name, files under /etc take precedence. This lets you customize behavior without editing package files, preserving upgrade safety. A common mistake is editing /usr/lib/service files directly; updates can overwrite your changes. Another useful location is /run/systemd/system for runtime units generated on the fly. Practically, when you create or edit a unit under /etc, always run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd rereads the files. If you forget daemon-reload you may see the old behavior and wonder why your changes didn't apply. Example: if nginx. service exists in both /usr/lib and /etc, the version in /etc will be used by systemd and symlinks in multi-user. target. wants will point to the effective unit. Unit file locations and precedence means /etc/systemd/system overrides /usr/lib/systemd/system; use /etc for customizations and run daemon-reload after edits.. In practical terms, where unit files live and which ones win when duplicated. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The systemctl tool is the primary interface for interacting with systemd. Learn a small set of commands that cover most tasks. Use systemctl start service to start a service immediately. Use systemctl stop service to stop it. Restart restarts a service, useful after a configuration change that cannot be reloaded. Reload asks the service to re-read its configuration without fully restarting; not every service supports reload. Use systemctl enable service to configure the service to start at boot; this creates a symlink under multi-user. target. wants. systemctl disable prevents automatic start at boot. To check runtime state, use systemctl status service which shows active/inactive, PID, recent journal lines, and whether the unit is enabled. Two helpful queries are systemctl is-active and systemctl is-enabled; they return concise information suited for scripts. A common confusion is thinking enable also starts the service immediately — enable only affects boot. If you want it running now, run start as well. Practice combining these commands when managing a sample service to internalize the lifecycle. Common systemctl commands means systemctl start/stop/restart/reload control runtime state; enable/disable control boot behavior; status and is-active/is-enabled report state.. In practical terms, start, stop, restart, reload, and check state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

systemctl status is the first command to run when a service misbehaves. It gives a concise snapshot: whether the unit is active or inactive, the main process PID, memory usage, and a few recent journal entries. Use this output to determine immediate causes, such as a crash on startup or a failed dependency. An important skill is reading the status summary and then following up with journalctl -u service for detailed logs. A common misinterpretation is assuming an inactive state always means the service crashed; some services stop after completing a oneshot task. Look at Type= in the unit to understand expected behavior. For example, if a service uses Type=forking, the main process may detach and status will show the child PID. Always combine status with the unit file and logs to build a diagnosis. Try running status, note the PID and recent messages, then open the journal to see complete entries for that unit. Inspecting status with systemctl status means systemctl status gives a quick diagnostic snapshot; use it with journalctl for full logs and unit file inspection for context.. In practical terms, interpret pid, active state, and journal excerpts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When systemctl status provides a brief window into recent events, journalctl supplies the full log history for a unit. Use journalctl -u service to see all messages generated by that service. You can add -n 20 to show the last twenty lines or --since to restrict by time. These logs include stdout and stderr emitted by the daemon plus messages from systemd itself. A typical. service file contains three main sections that tell systemd how to treat the service. The [Unit] section holds metadata such as Description= and dependency directives like After= and Requires=. Use After= to ensure the service starts after a given target, for example After=network. target. The [Service] section defines the runtime behavior. Key directives include Type= to describe the process model, ExecStart= for the start command, ExecStop= or ExecReload= when needed, WorkingDirectory= to set the process working directory, and User= or Group= to drop privileges. The Restart= directive controls automatic restarts, for example Restart=on-failure. The [Install] section specifies how the unit is enabled; WantedBy=multi-user. target will make the service start in the typical multi-user environment. A common oversight is placing ExecStart without a full path; always provide the absolute path to avoid PATH-related failures. Reading and editing these three sections gives you direct control over service lifecycle and security. Within the [Service] section a few directives determine how a service runs and how systemd treats it. ExecStart is the command systemd runs to start the service; it should be a full path to the executable or script. Type tells systemd how the service behaves on startup. Type=simple assumes the process stays in the foreground; Type=forking expects the service to fork and background itself; Type=oneshot is for short-lived tasks. User and Group drop privileges so the service runs as a non-root account when appropriate, increasing security. Restart controls automatic restarts; Restart=on-failure restarts only on error exits, while Restart=always will restart for any exit. Choosing improper combinations causes confusion: for example, using Type=forking but pointing ExecStart to a script that does not fork will lead to incorrect PID detection. Always pair your Type setting with the actual process model of the daemon. Example: a simple logging script used as a service often uses Type=simple and runs in the foreground so systemd can manage it cleanly. A frequent source of confusion is making changes to unit files and then not seeing those changes take effect. After creating or editing any unit under /etc or elsewhere, you must run sudo systemctl daemon-reload so systemd rereads its configuration files. Without this reload, systemd continues to use its cached view and will not know about new units or modifications. If a unit still fails to start after daemon-reload, follow this checklist: 1) Run systemctl status to get the short diagnostic. 2) Run journalctl -u to read detailed logs. 3) Inspect the unit file for absolute paths in ExecStart and correct Type. 4) Check file permissions and the executable bit on scripts. 5) If you enabled the service, confirm the symlink under multi-user. target. wants. A common operational mistake is enabling a broken unit and then rebooting, which can lead to boot-time failures. For custom or critical services, test start/stop behavior locally before enabling at boot. Managing services requires awareness of operational risk. The most important safety tip is never to stop or disable critical services like sshd when you have no alternative access to the machine. If you are connected over SSH and you stop sshd, you will be disconnected and may be locked out. Always have a secondary access method, such as a console or out-of-band management, before touching remote-critical services. When you create a temporary service for testing, plan a cleanup path: sudo systemctl stop my-custom-service, sudo systemctl disable my-custom-service, then remove the script and unit file from /usr/local/bin and /etc/systemd/system. Finally run sudo systemctl daemon-reload to purge the removed unit from systemd's view. A common mistake is leaving test services enabled which will persist across reboots. Cleaning up prevents unexpected behavior later and keeps system targets uncluttered. Think through the impact of each enable or disable action before running the command on production systems. Second, systemctl is the control tool: start, stop, restart, reload for runtime actions, and enable or disable for boot-time behavior. Third, unit file locations matter: files under /etc/systemd/system override those provided in /usr/lib/systemd/system.
